items.title: Lumen Announces AI Networking, Quantum Research and PQC Plans
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Lumen Technologies announced three initiatives focused on energy-aware AI networking with Emerald AI, research into quantum connectivity with The Ohio State University, and post-quantum security capabilities through its Fortinet-based SASE solution.

Lumen and Emerald AI are exploring a pilot to route AI inference workloads to locations based on power availability, cost, latency, security and network performance.

Lumen is funding research into long-distance quantum networking and distributed sensing, while planning to add Fortinet post-quantum cryptography capabilities to its SASE offering, with initial availability targeted for November 2026 and general availability for January 2027.

PRESS RELEASE — Lumen Technologies (Nasdaq: LUMN) today announced three new initiatives using intelligent networking to address AI energy challenges, future quantum connectivity, and emerging security threats. As enterprises’ AI and quantum ambition begin to outgrow traditional networks, Lumen is turning its network into an active platform for innovation—combining fiber connectivity scale, programmable control, software intelligence, and a connected ecosystem of partners to help enable the next generation of computing.

With Emerald AI , Lumen’s intelligent network enables AI workloads to automatically shift to alternate locations based on power availability, cost, and other factors.

Lumen is investing in research at The Ohio State University to explore how its fiber infrastructure could support quantum connectivity over distances.

items.title: v5.22.0: Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk)
items.summary:
New Models

Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk)

Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's largest and most capable model to date: a 1 trillion-parameter natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 49 billion active parameters per token (52 billion including embeddings and output layers), trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral's own datacenters in Europe.

Mistral Large 4 unifies instruction following, reasoning, coding, and agentic workflows in a single set of weights. While a generalist model, it shows especially good performance on workloads such as cybersecurity, finance, and law, and it surpasses frontier closed models on visual grounding. It is natively fluent in 160+ languages, including every official language of the European Union.

Key Features

Mistral Large 4 includes the following architectural choices:

~1T total / ~52B active parameters : granular Mixture-of-Experts with 128 routed experts (4 active per token) and 1 shared expert.

items.title: Alice & Bob Estimates 22,593 Qubits to Break RSA-2048
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Alice & Bob researchers estimate that running Shor’s algorithm against RSA-2048 would require 22,593 physical cat qubits and 3.14 days on fault-tolerant superconducting quantum hardware.

The study estimates that attacking the 256-bit elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem would require 29,588 physical qubits and 61.8 minutes, with the results based on cat-qubit hardware, LDPC-cat codes and a redesigned adder.

The estimates are theoretical resource projections rather than demonstrations of cryptographic attacks, and Alice & Bob recommends that organizations begin migrating to post-quantum cryptography as research continues to reduce projected hardware requirements.

PRESS RELEASE — Alice & Bob, a leader in fault-tolerant quantum computing, sets a record low for the total quantum resources (qubits multiplied by runtime) required to run Shor’s algorithm on today’s encryption. Its cat-qubit architecture needs 40 times fewer physical qubits than Google Quantum AI’s Craig Gidney 2025 estimate to break RSA-2048 ( arxiv).

In the paper “Shor’s algorithm compiled on cat qubits: 22 593 qubits for RSA-2048 in 3.14 days” (IACR ePrint) researchers estimate the resources to break the following systems on fault-tolerant superconducting cat-qubit hardware:

RSA-2048: 22,593 physical qubits, 3.14 days. RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring large integers. It is one of the world’s most widely used public-key systems, securing much of the internet, from online banking to email and digital signatures.

items.title: E.ON and Qoro Test Hybrid Quantum Computing for Energy Scheduling
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Qoro, E.ON and the UK National Quantum Computing Centre developed a proof of concept using hybrid quantum-classical computing to improve peer-to-peer energy transaction scheduling.

The team used Qoro’s Divi SDK and scheduler to decompose large grid optimisation problems into subproblems of up to 50 qubits, reducing quantum hardware execution time by approximately threefold through spatial circuit packing on IBM hardware.

The research found that QAOA sampling combined with classical feasibility repair reduced residual decomposition error compared with classical baselines, although the results remain a proof of concept rather than a demonstrated deployment in an operational power grid.

PRESS RELEASE — Qoro, E.ON , and the UK National Quantum Computing Centre (NQCC) have successfully developed a proof-of-concept, exploring future applications of hybrid quantum-classical computing in peer-to-peer energy trading. With SparQ grant funding, the team developed a new decomposition-based optimisation pipeline, built using Qoro’s open-source software development kit (SDK), Divi, and orchestrated through Qoro’s scheduler. The resulting proof-of-concept improved upon previous hybrid methods using energy grid benchmark models, outperforming classical baselines. It also reduced hardware execution time by approximately 3x through spatial circuit packing on IBM quantum hardware. This proves that software orchestration can unlock utility-scale applications on today’s quantum processors.

By mathematically breaking the massive grid optimisation problem into smaller, more manageable pieces, the algorithm could reduce the energy transaction scheduling rounds (by reducing the solution decomposition length) to achieve high solution accuracy. In a real-world application, the solution decomposition length acts as ‘scheduling rounds’ that plan and coordinate energy transactions between grid users. By proving that the number of required rounds can be drastically reduced, these findings offer a near-term pathway for power grids to more efficiently manage complex energy transaction scheduling and ease grid strain.

This project was conducted with oversight from the STFC Hartree Centre and the NQCC through the SparQ 2025 programme, a UK national initiative supporting industry-led quantum computing projects focused on real-world applications. Earlier research by E.ON and the Hartree Centre laid the groundwork for this collaboration.

items.title: Niels Bohr Institute Spinout Pelagic Systems Targets Quantum Hardware Control
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Pelagic Systems, a spinout from the Novo Nordisk Foundation Quantum Computing Programme at the Niels Bohr Institute, is launching software for calibrating, monitoring and controlling quantum hardware.

The company says its platform has been demonstrated on superconducting quantum processors, where it can characterize and recalibrate key processor parameters on millisecond timescales.

Supported by Innovation Fund Denmark, Pelagic is offering its software to research groups and quantum computing companies working on advanced quantum hardware.

Pelagic Systems, a new spinout from the Novo Nordisk Foundation Quantum Computing Programme (NQCP) at the Niels Bohr Institute , was announced on October 27, 2026, according to a company press release. The company is developing the software layer for operating quantum hardware at the frontier.

Pelagic describes quantum processors as experimental systems that are delicate and constantly changing. Its platform brings tools to measure, understand and control them into a single software package, the release states. The company says that by closely integrating high-level experimental software with real-time hardware control, the platform makes possible a new generation of quantum experiments that can respond, adapt and explore the full potential of quantum hardware.

For Peter Krogstrup, CEO of NQCP and Quantum Foundry Copenhagen , Pelagic is an example of how technology developed around the programme’s quantum computing work can become capabilities with value well beyond a single research project, the release says. Krogstrup said in the release:

items.title: IQM Demonstrates Entanglement Across a Complete 54-Qubit Processor
items.summary:
Insider Brief

IQM Quantum Computers reports that its cloud-accessible Emerald system has achieved a Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) entangled state across all 54 qubits simultaneously.

The company measured a fidelity of 0.516 across the full processor with readout error mitigation applied, exceeding the 0.500 threshold cited for distinguishing genuine entanglement from noise.

IQM attributes the result to improvements in calibration, gate selection and automated state preparation, and says cloud customers can access the system’s full-chip performance.

PRESS RELEASE — IQM Quantum Computers (Nasdaq: IQMX), a global leader in superconducting quantum computers, today announced that its cloud-accessible IQM Emerald system has fully entangled all 54 qubits on the chip simultaneously, a result that shows the system’s computational quality holds up when every qubit is put to work at once. IQM’s cloud customers now have access to that same full-chip performance, so their computations can draw on the entire processor rather than a fraction of it.

These results rank among the strongest reported for any commercially available quantum computer, giving customers access to state-of-the-art, high-quality processors. Until now, a user running a comparable demonstration on IQM Emerald could reliably use on the order of 30 qubits within a single algorithm. Studies on large quantum chips often use only a fraction of the available qubits, commonly 10 to 20, even when the hardware has many more. Emerald’s result shows the alternative: an entire processor working together on one computation.

“Entangling the entire chip means every qubit and every connection between them has to work correctly in the same circuit. Getting there came down to being smarter about how we prepare the state itself, choosing the gate order to keep idle time to a minimum,” said Craig Ciesla, CTO, IQM Quantum Computers. “Our current and prospective cloud customers now have the chance to benefit from the same tools and system performance that made this achievement possible.”

items.title: Pasqal’s 256-Qubit Processor Finds Unexpected Quantum Magnet Behavior
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Pasqal and its research collaborators used a 256-qubit neutral-atom processor to study a two-dimensional quantum magnet and observed an unexpected slowdown in its relaxation after a sudden change.

The slowdown appeared in a regime where three classical simulation methods diverged from one another and the experimental results, although the researchers have not yet explained the behavior.

The findings, published as an arXiv preprint, suggest quantum processors could help investigate complex physical systems that challenge existing simulation methods, but do not demonstrate computational quantum advantage.

PRESS RELEASE — Pasqal (Nasdaq: PSQL), a global leader in neutral-atom quantum computing, today announced that its 256-qubit quantum processor has revealed an unexpected behavior in a two-dimensional quantum magnet: under certain conditions, the system takes far longer to settle after being disturbed than theory predicts. The results, released as a preprint with the Flatiron Institute, the University of Augsburg, Forschungszentrum Jülich, the University of Regensburg and the Institut d’Optique–CNRS, were obtained in a regime where three state-of-the-art classical simulation methods no longer agree with one another.

A regime theory cannot yet predict

The researchers abruptly pushed the magnet out of equilibrium, a sudden change physicists call a quench and   expected it to settle quickly into a new stable state, as most systems do. Under one set of conditions, it didn’t. The result marks a shift in how quantum processors can be used in research: not only to reproduce what scientists already know, but to reveal behavior they did not anticipate.

items.title: Nord Quantique Secures $10 Million DARPA Funding Extension
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Nord Quantique has secured a US$10 million extension to its DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative Stage B agreement to continue evaluation of its quantum computing architecture.

The company uses bosonic quantum error correction to protect quantum information within physical qubits, with the aim of reducing the hardware overhead required for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

DARPA ’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative evaluates whether emerging quantum architectures can reach utility-scale operation by 2033, while Nord Quantique says the funding will support its development roadmap.

PRESS RELEASE — Nord Quantique , a Canadian quantum computing company pioneering hardware-efficient quantum error correction, today announced a US$10 million extension of its Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s (DARPA) Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (QBI) Stage B agreement.

The extension supports Nord Quantique ’s continued participation in Stage B and its potential to deliver utility-scale quantum computing with significantly reduced hardware requirements.

DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative aims to determine whether emerging quantum computing architectures can achieve utility-scale operation by 2033. The program rigorously evaluates the technical feasibility, scalability and resources required to develop commercially valuable quantum computers.

items.title: Shionogi Wins NEDO Award for Quantum-Assisted Drug Discovery
items.summary:
Insider Brief

D-Wave customer Shionogi has won first place in the Quality of Life category of Japan’s NEDO Challenge for research applying quantum computing to drug discovery.

A peer-reviewed study published in Scientific Reports in July 2026 found that a quantum-assisted generative AI model produced 97% chemically valid molecular representations, compared with 73% for an equivalent classical model.

The ¥40 million award will support Shionogi’s continued research combining quantum computing and classical high-performance computing to generate and evaluate potential drug candidates.

PRESS RELEASE — D-Wave Quantum Inc. (NASDAQ: QBTS) (“ D-Wave “), the only dual-platform quantum computing company providing both annealing and gate-model systems, software and services, today announced that its customer Shionogi & Co., Ltd. (“Shionogi”) has won first place in the Quality of Life (QOL) category of the NEDO Challenge for its research exploring the application of quantum computing to drug discovery. The award-winning research includes, among other achievements, a peer-reviewed study published in Scientific Reports in July 2026, which integrated D-Wave annealing quantum computing technology into a generative AI model for molecular design.

Among the achievements included in the award-winning peer-reviewed research, conducted in collaboration with D-Wave , was that 97% of molecular representations generated by the quantum-assisted model were chemically valid, compared with 73% using an equivalent classical model. The quantum-assisted model also generated a higher proportion of molecules with strong drug-likeness scores, exceeding both the classical model and the training dataset. These findings demonstrate how annealing quantum computing could improve the quality of generative AI outputs for early-stage drug discovery.

The ¥40 million NEDO prize will support Shionogi’s continued research into applying quantum computing to one of the pharmaceutical industry’s most complex challenges: designing promising new drug candidate molecules. The award recognized Shionogi’s broader quantum-assisted drug discovery research, which combines D-Wave quantum computing and classical high-performance computing approaches to generate and evaluate drug candidate molecules.

items.title: Researchers Curb Unwanted Transitions in Ultrafast Quantum Gates
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Researchers from Jülich, Aachen and Cologne performed single-qubit operations in 6.8 nanoseconds with accuracies exceeding 99.98%, demonstrating fast, precise control of a superconducting qubit.

Their R2D pulse-shaping method reduced unwanted multiphoton transitions by more than 20 times compared with the established DRAG method.

Tests used a single isolated transmon qubit, with further experiments needed to assess performance in larger processors and two-qubit operations.

Image: Quantum computer laboratory at the Peter Grünberg Institute for Functional Quantum Systems (PGI-13) at Forschungszentrum Jülich. (Forschungszentrum Jülich / Sascha Kreklau)

PRESS RELEASE — Researchers from Jülich, Aachen and Cologne have performed a quantum operation on a qubit in just 6.8 nanoseconds – with more than 99.98 percent accuracy. Such operations typically take several tens of nanoseconds in superconducting quantum computers. The paper was published in Nature Communications .

6.8 nanoseconds – that’s how long it takes light to travel a distance of around two metres in a vacuum. In this tiny fraction of a second, researchers in the Peter Grünberg Institute for Functional Quantum Systems (PGI-13) and Quantum Control (PGI-8) at Forschungszentrum Jülich have succeeded in performing elementary computing operations on a quantum bit, or qubit for short.

items.summary:
Day-0 vLLM support for Mistral Large 4 with sparse MLA, cross-layer KV sharing, DSpark speculative decoding, DCP/PCP long context and NIXL P/D on NVIDIA Blackwell.

We're excited to announce day-0 support for Mistral Large 4 in vLLM. Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's new frontier mixture-of-experts native multimodal model. It combines a DeepSeek-style sparse attention stack (MLA plus a DSA top-k indexer) with several new architecture features: cross-layer KV sharing, NoPE layers, SSMax and LeRoPE. items.title: Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face
items.summary:
Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter , and a context window of 1M tokens .

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection .

items.title: Hogan Lovells Cadwalader Advises Intel in Pending Acquisition of Classiq Technologies
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Intel agreed to acquire quantum computing software provider Classiq Technologies, with legal advice from Hogan Lovells Cadwalader.

The proposed acquisition would combine Classiq ’s software synthesis platform with Intel ’s spin-qubit manufacturing and existing software to create a full-stack quantum computing platform.

The deal would position Intel to add quantum processing units to its portfolio of CPUs, GPUs and application-specific integrated circuits.

PRESS RELEASE — Global law firm Hogan Lovells Cadwalader advised Intel Corporation (Nasdaq: INTC) as it entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Classiq Technologies Ltd, a leading provider of quantum computing software.

The combination of Classiq ’s synthesis platform with Intel ’s spin-qubit manufacturing and existing software would create a user-friendly full-stack quantum computing platform, enabling the promising technology to mature into a mainstream computing business.

The combination would enable Intel to become a full-stack quantum solutions provider, while also allowing the company to add Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) to its already diverse compute platform portfolio spanning Central Processing Units (CPUs), Graphical Processing Units (GPUs) and application-specific integrated circuit (ASICs).

items.title: PsiQuantum Unveils Optical Circuit Switch for AI Data Centers
items.summary:
Insider Brief

PsiQuantum has unveiled an 8×8 optical circuit switching demonstration built on its low-loss silicon photonics platform, originally developed for utility-scale quantum computing.

Company testing reported 1.2 dB insertion loss, 40 dB crosstalk performance and less than 3 milliseconds of reconfiguration time, without optical amplification.

PsiQuantum is sharing demonstration samples with selected prospective customers and plans to develop commercial products for AI data center connectivity while continuing its work on fault-tolerant quantum computers.

PRESS RELEASE — PsiQuantum today unveiled its Optical Circuit Switching (OCS) technology, demonstrating how the company’s advanced, low-loss silicon photonics platform can be applied to some of the most significant scaling challenges facing AI infrastructure.

AI systems are scaling faster than computing infrastructure, with increasingly large pools of compute placing enormous demands on the networks connecting them. As moving data efficiently between these systems becomes a fundamental constraint for continued AI scaling, the computing industry is increasingly turning to optics to provide faster, more efficient, and scalable connectivity.

PsiQuantum ‘s first publicly disclosed OCS is an 8×8-radix demonstration vehicle built on the low-loss, silicon photonics platform that the company has spent nearly a decade developing for utility-scale quantum computing. Testing conducted in PsiQuantum’s labs has shown typical results of 1.2 dB of insertion loss, 40 dB cross talk, and less than 3 ms of reconfiguration time, all exceeding initial targets set for these devices and without amplification.

items.title: NVision and HyperLight Partner to Develop Photonic Quantum Chips
items.summary:
Insider Brief

NVision has announced a peer-reviewed Nature paper on individually addressable organic molecular spin-photon interfaces and a partnership with HyperLight to integrate molecular qubits onto thin-film lithium niobate photonic integrated circuits.

The companies aim to combine NVision ’s molecular qubits with HyperLight’s photonic chip technology to develop quantum hardware with optical connections between qubits and compatibility with established foundry manufacturing processes.

NVision is targeting a demonstration of on-chip performance by the end of 2026, with its longer-term roadmap aiming for 1,000 physical qubits and then 1,000 logical qubits by 2030.

PRESS RELEASE — NVision , a quantum technology company, announced the publication of landmark peer-reviewed research in Nature and a strategic partnership with HyperLight Corporation (“HyperLight”), an industry leader in thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) photonics. The companies will integrate NVision ’s thin-film molecular qubits directly onto advanced photonic integrated circuits (PICs). Together, these milestones establish a practical path to quantum computing at scale, using photonic connectivity to link quantum resources within and across processors. This opens a path toward millions of qubits on chips compatible with standard foundry manufacturing.

The Nature publication confirms the first ever individually addressable organic molecular spin-photon interface, which is the key ingredient for connecting stationary qubits with photons. Until now, molecular spins could not be individually and coherently controlled, preventing them from serving as true qubits. That barrier has now been broken: the core building block can be controlled at the single-molecule level. This opens a new path to scale, where molecular qubits can be deposited as thin films, much like OLED materials, directly on top of PICs, turning established photonic chip technology into a platform for scaling quantum computers.

“This proves what we’ve long believed: that organic chemistry offers a fundamentally better building block for quantum,” said Dr. Sella Brosh, CEO of NVision . “For years, the industry has been locked in a hardware race using modalities that would require decades and multi-billion-dollar proprietary fabrication facilities to achieve scale. With the creation of the world’s first manufacturable organic qubit, we now enter quantum’s molecular era, establishing a new architecture based on photonic connectivity from the get-go, with a clear path to scale through existing foundry infrastructure.”

items.title: UbiQD Wins New Mexico Grant for Quantum Light Source Development
items.summary:
Insider Brief

UbiQD has secured a New Mexico Technology & Innovation Office grant to develop a quantum dot-based light source designed to produce individual photons reliably at room temperature for quantum computing applications.

The project will fund optical equipment and device prototyping at UbiQD’s Los Alamos headquarters, building on earlier research with Los Alamos National Laboratory into single-photon emission from cadmium-, lead- and mercury-free quantum dots.

UbiQD is also developing its intellectual property portfolio, which the company says includes 17 granted U.S. patents, 23 granted international patents and 27 pending applications, including a patent for a fiber-coupled broadband light source

PRESS RELEASE — UbiQD, Inc ., a global leader in quantum dot technology and manufacturing, has received a $200,000 grant through New Mexico’s Quantum Technologies Award  from the Economic Development New Mexico (EDNM) Department through its Technology and Innovation Office (TIO). The grant funds development of a key component for quantum computers and ultra-secure quantum communication networks: a specialized light source, connected directly to a fiber optic cable, that emits single particles of light, one at a time, on demand.

Most of today’s quantum computers store information in superconducting circuits that must be chilled to a fraction of a degree above absolute zero inside large, expensive refrigerators. Another approach uses individual particles of light, called photons, to carry information. Photons can travel efficiently over long distances, which also makes them the natural choice for secure quantum communication networks, and light-based systems need far less extreme cooling. However, they do depend on a special light source that produces exactly one photon at a time, on demand. Typical light sources either emit a plurality photons at random, wasting most of their output, or must themselves be cooled to near absolute zero.

Nothing available today addresses all the needs: safe materials, room temperature operation (not inside expensive refrigeration systems), tunable emission, fiber optic cable-coupled, and reliability at scale. UbiQD has spent a decade developing quantum dot technology, and researchers have shown in published studies that this class of materials can do exactly what quantum hardware companies need.

items.title: D-Wave and LG CNS Partner on Quantum Optimization in South Korea
items.summary:
Insider Brief

D-Wave Quantum and South Korea’s LG CNS have signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to advance quantum optimization applications in South Korea and international markets.

The companies plan to combine D-Wave ’s quantum annealing technology with LG CNS’s mathematical optimization and systems integration expertise to develop applications for manufacturing, telecommunications, finance and retail.

The collaboration aims to move quantum optimization projects from proof of concept toward production, with potential applications in factory scheduling, delivery routing and resource allocation.

PRESS RELEASE — D-Wave Quantum Inc. (NASDAQ: QBTS) (“ D-Wave ” or the “Company”), the only dual-platform quantum computing company providing both annealing and gate-model systems, software and services, and LG CNS Co., Ltd. (“LG CNS”), a leading AI transformation company in South Korea, today announced that the companies have signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding (“MOU”) to advance the adoption of quantum computing for enterprise optimization in South Korea and international markets. The collaboration will focus on applying D-Wave’s annealing quantum computing technology to complex optimization challenges, with the goal of moving applications from proof of concept into production.

D-Wave CEO Dr. Alan Baratz and LG CNS President and CEO Hyun Shin-Gyoon announced the MOU onstage at D-Wave’s Qubits Asia conference in Seoul today. The companies intend to combine D-Wave’s annealing quantum computing technologies with LG CNS’s industry expertise, mathematical optimization capabilities and systems integration experience to develop applications for customers in manufacturing, telecommunications, finance and retail. The companies also intend to pursue joint go-to-market opportunities.

LG CNS brings extensive mathematical optimization expertise across industries, including manufacturing and the public sector, with end-to-end capabilities spanning problem definition, mathematical modeling, algorithm validation and real-world implementation. LG CNS has also been conducting research on applying mathematical optimization and quantum computing to real-world industrial challenges, including image reconstruction and inspection and the detection of underground anomalies.

items.title: Qarakal Quantum And Quantum Elements Receive BIRD Foundation Grant For Quantum Computing Innovation With a $2.4 Million Budget
items.summary:

Quantum Elements and Qarakal Quantum were selected by the BIRD Foundation for a $2.4 million project to develop a quantum simulation platform for chemical reactions on material surfaces.

The collaboration will combine Qarakal’s superconducting quantum hardware with Quantum Elements’ digital-twin software and error-management tools to jointly optimize hardware and chemistry workflows.

The companies aim to build a validated prototype, benchmark chemistry models and quantum algorithms to investigate how quantum computing could complement existing catalyst simulation methods.

PRESS RELEASE — Quantum Elements and Qarakal Quantum today announced they have been selected by the Israel-U.S. Binational Industrial Research and Development (BIRD) Foundation to jointly develop a quantum simulation platform for understanding and designing the chemical reactions that occur on material surfaces.

The project, one of seven approved by the BIRD Foundation, has a budget of $2.4 million.

The project will combine Qarakal Quantum’s modular superconducting quantum hardware and hardware-software co-design approach with Quantum Elements’ software for advancing fault-tolerant quantum computing, using AI-driven co-design, error suppression, error correction and decoders.

items.title: Guest Post: Why Dedicated Compute Matters for AI and Quantum Computing
items.summary:
Guest Post By Christopher Miglino, CEO, Axe Compute

Every dollar going into AI infrastructure today is also a bet on what comes after it. Compute has become a strategic resource. Companies are spending billions to secure the processing power to build, train and run AI, and we’re still early: much of the global economy hasn’t put AI into its core operations yet.

But the infrastructure being built for AI is also the ground quantum will eventually stand on. That raises real questions about security, control and how to invest for a world where very different technologies run side by side.

My answer is dedicated compute. Enterprise AI customers already demand it, and it’s the flexibility businesses will need as quantum matures.

For most of the past decade, cloud economics favored sharing. Pooling resources across customers let providers reach scale, lift utilization and put sophisticated compute within reach of companies that couldn’t fund it upfront. That model works, and it will keep serving an enormous market.

But the math changes when compute becomes the thing your business runs on.

Picture a bank building proprietary trading models, or a pharmaceutical company running computational research. Their intellectual property lives in those workloads, alongside strict demands on performance, security and compliance. Their compute has become the business itself.

items.title: IonQ Receives $7.5 Million from AFRL for Quantum Networking
items.summary:
Insider Brief

IonQ has received $7.5 million in Phase 2 funding from the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) to expand a quantum network previously delivered in Rome, New York.

The upgrades include free-space optical links, quantum frequency converters, upgraded network hardware and automated control software to support connections between different quantum systems.

The work aims to support quantum communications across standard telecommunications infrastructure and open air, advancing AFRL’s plans for interoperable quantum networks in metropolitan and defense environments.

PRESS RELEASE — IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), the world’s leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, today announced it has received $7.5 million in follow-on funding from the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL). The Phase 2 contract expands upon the first-generation quantum network IonQ previously delivered in Rome, New York. The collaboration explores key optical, hardware, and software layers to turn the deployment into an operational, interoperable research platform.

Phase 1 established the core physical network foundation. Phase 2 equips AFRL with additional capabilities needed to connect different types of quantum hardware across non-laboratory environments. Classical routers and fiber-optic cables allow different computers to share data across the internet. Similarly, these new full-stack enhancements allow connectivity of distinct quantum systems and route quantum communication over standard telecommunications infrastructure and open air.

“This follow-on funding from AFRL underscores the strength of our long-term partnership and validates IonQ ‘s full-stack approach. We are unlocking new domains for quantum networking by going to free space optics,” said Jordan Shapiro, IonQ President, Quantum Platform. “Advanced optical hardware and automated control software are what close the gap between laboratory demonstration and field deployment. We are building quantum networking that runs on standard telecom infrastructure and through open air, and proving it on a live network.”

items.title: Zumo and Quantum Chain Partner on Quantum-Resilient Finance
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Zumo and Quantum Chain have signed a memorandum of understanding to explore quantum-resilient infrastructure for UK digital assets and blockchain-based financial services.

The collaboration will examine applications across private networks, tokenised deposits, payments and institutional digital assets, including a potential quantum-resistant GBP stablecoin subject to regulatory requirements.

The companies aim to support cryptographic agility and post-quantum security for financial institutions as concerns grow about future quantum computers that could compromise current public-key cryptography.

PRESS RELEASE — Crypto-as-a-service platform Zumo has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Quantum Chain , a quantum-resilient blockchain and infrastructure platform, with the companies uniting to help safeguard the UK’s developing digital assets sector against the spectre of future quantum threats.

There are growing fears regarding the imminence of Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computers (CRQCs) that will soon be able to break standard public-key cryptography that underpins blockchain security, asset ownership, and institutional custody.

In response, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) is advising financial institutions to ensure they are completely migrated to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) by 2035 . Most estimates point to the 2030s for ‘Q-Day’, which will herald the arrival of CRQCs powerful enough to break public-key encryption standards using algorithms like Shor’s algorithm.

items.title: Pasqal Launches AI Workflow for Cloud Quantum Experiments
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Pasqal has launched an AI-assisted workflow on Pasqal Cloud that helps users turn scientific ideas or published protocols into experiments executed on quantum processing units (QPUs).

The workflow coordinates protocol formalization, quantum job preparation, emulation-based validation, cloud submission and processing of results into scientific observables.

The plugin works with agentic coding environments including Claude Code, Cursor and Codex, and supports three Pasqal Cloud QPUs in France, Canada and Saudi Arabia.

PRESS RELEASE — Pasqal (Nasdaq: PSQL), a global leader in neutral-atom quantum computing, today announced the availability of an AI-assisted workflow on Pasqal Cloud. Available as a plugin for leading agentic coding environments, the new feature can take a well-defined scientific idea to a running experiment on a quantum processing unit (QPU), significantly reducing the engineering effort that has long stood between an idea for a quantum use case and its execution on hardware.

As quantum computers become easier to access through the cloud, the challenge is shifting from hardware availability to how researchers design, run and interpret quantum experiments. Translating a protocol into a hardware-ready job still requires specialized engineering expertise and significant time. As a result, many promising ideas go untested, even when suitable hardware exists.

The AI-assisted workflow orchestrates the full pipeline. Starting from an experiment described in a paper or conceived as an original idea, it extracts or formalizes the protocol, translates it into a hardware-ready quantum job, validates it in emulation, submits it through the cloud and processes the results into scientific observables.

items.title: What NIST’s Post-Quantum Cryptography Plan Means For Companies And Their Suppliers
items.summary:
Insider Brief

NIST’s post-quantum cryptography transition report outlines a migration requiring coordinated changes across enterprise software, hardware, identity systems and technology suppliers.

Prioritized sensitive federal systems must adopt quantum-resistant key establishment by the end of 2030 and digital signatures by the end of 2031, ahead of the broader 2035 migration target.

Organizations must assess data confidentiality needs, supplier readiness and equipment lifespans, while hybrid cryptography can add complexity and require a second migration.

Companies buying software, renewing cloud contracts or designing connected devices may be making decisions that determine whether their systems can withstand a future quantum attack.

That is one of the practical implications of the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s new report on the transition to post-quantum cryptography, or PQC. The agency’s road map describes a migration that reaches beyond security departments into procurement, product development and the technology suppliers on which organizations depend.

The challenge is timing. Information that needs to remain confidential for years could be collected today and decrypted later by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Meanwhile, replacing the cryptography protecting that information could require coordinated changes across software, hardware and identity systems.

items.title: Intel’s Classiq Deal May Signal a Pivot From Quiet Quantum Effort To Active Commercialization
items.summary:
Insider Brief

Intel ’s proposed acquisition of Classiq would move its decade-long quantum research effort toward commercialization by combining its hardware and manufacturing capabilities with Classiq ’s software and enterprise customers.

Intel plans to maintain Classiq ’s support for competing quantum hardware while exploring manufacturing and component partnerships with other quantum companies.

The companies expect the acquisition to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals, but provided no firm timetable for profitability or commercially useful quantum systems at scale.

Intel , a pioneer in quantum computing, has been relatively quiet about its technology and nearly silent about how it is pursing commercialization.

That silence has been shattered.

Intel executives said during a media briefing Tuesday that it is moving to turn more than a decade of quantum computing research into a business with its proposed acquisition of Classiq , adding software and enterprise customers to a hardware effort that has largely stayed out of the commercial spotlight.

items.title: 247A, Notes 3: Singular integral operators
items.summary:

items.title: NIST Report Provides Guidelines for Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards
items.summary:
Insider Brief

NIST has released a road map outlining how organizations should replace quantum-vulnerable cryptography with post-quantum standards, including transition timelines and planning considerations.

Federal migration targets include 2035 for most systems, with earlier deadlines of 2030 for key establishment and 2031 for digital signatures in high-value assets and high-impact systems.

The report encourages organizations to assess their cryptographic supply chains, prioritize sensitive data vulnerable to future decryption and consider hybrid approaches combining conventional and post-quantum cryptography.

Image: J. Wang/NIST and Shutterstock

PRESS RELEASE — In August 2024, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) released post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards made to withstand the assault of a future quantum computer. Now, the agency has released its high-level road map to help organizations switch to these standards.

The report, Transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography Standards (NISTIR 8547) , outlines NIST’s official approach and timelines for transitioning away from quantum-vulnerable algorithms to quantum-resistant standards. It is the core technical document meant to inform federal agencies, industry partners and standards organizations about what needs to change and when during the migration to PQC standards — a cryptographic modernization with details that will vary by organization but timelines that apply broadly.

items.title: Optimal quantum discrimination at Liouvillian exceptional points
items.summary:
Central to non-Hermitian sensing is the question of whether exceptional points (EPs) can make weak perturbations easier to detect.

We show that despite enhanced spectral response, in finite-dimensional Lindblad systems with a unique stationary state and a nonzero relaxation gap, EPs offer no fundamental advantage in how the observation time required for reliable detection of a weak perturbation scales with the perturbation strength.

We nevertheless demonstrate that by selectively choosing perturbations that enhance the quantum Fisher information rate, EPs can shorten the observation time needed to reach a predefined detection accuracy relative to a comparable non-EP reference at the same decay rate.

As an illustration, we show using an optomechanical model at an EP that we can detect a weak force through the cavity output at the same reliability in less time than a non-EP reference.

Our results establish fundamental limits on perturbation detection at EPs and can guide the design of faster non-Hermitian sensors based on optomechanical resonators, superconducting qubits, and trapped ions.

items.title: Hodge--Riemann relations for nef bundles
items.summary:
We introduce the $(m,p,q)$-Lefschetz property for $(1,1)$-type endomorphisms of Hodge--Lefschetz modules, providing a framework for studying nef $(1,1)$-classes and characteristic classes of nef vector bundles on compact Kähler manifolds. Under a Hall--Rado type condition on nef twisted vector bundles, we prove Hodge--Riemann relations for products of top Chern classes and, in suitable bidegrees, for products of derived Schur classes.

For products of nef $(1,1)$-classes, we show furthermore that the Hall--Rado type condition is equivalent to simultaneous Hodge--Riemann relations. Our proofs build on the purity theorem and descent lemma of Cattani, Kaplan, and Schmid.

We extend the descent lemma to Schur classes of nef vector bundles. We also establish formal analogs for projective bundle modules over Hodge--Lefschetz modules, with applications to tautological classes and descent on matroid Chow rings.

items.title: Multi-State Linear Attention with Generalized Second-Order Routing
items.summary:
Self-attention plays a key role in long-sequence modeling, but its quadratic time complexity fundamentally limits the scaling of Large Language Models. Recently, Multi-State Linear Attention (MSLA) mechanisms have been proposed to make sequence modeling more efficient by splitting the context into segments and compressing each in its own memory state.

MSLA aggregates the information extracted from each memory state using only the mean alignment between a query and each segment's keys, ignoring how the alignment is distributed within the segment. In order to model the relevance of a segment to a query more comprehensively and incorporate the variance of the alignment in the aggregation, we propose MERLIN (MomEnt Routing for multi-state LINear attention), a method that tracks the first and second moments of each segment's keys.

Using the moments of keys, a query can recover both the mean and the variance of its alignment with each segment to perform a more content-aware aggregation of per-state readouts. Experiments on multi-state variants of Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and Mamba-2-780M show that MERLIN consistently outperforms existing aggregation methods on various long-context tasks.

In particular, MERLIN outperforms baselines on RULER needle-in-a-haystack and long-context QA (+8.3% for Gated DeltaNet-1.3B and +7.0% for Mamba-2-780M) and diverse subtasks in LongBench (+13.5% and +12.0%). It even outperforms baselines that consume 4x more memory.

MERLIN provides a simple and general routing mechanism for improving long-context capabilities of MSLA models.

items.title: Algebraic fiberings of right-angled Coxeter groups on bipartite cone graphs
items.summary:
We study systems of moves and states in the sense of [JNW21] on certain bipartite graphs, and the associated homomorphisms from the commutator subgroups of right-angled Coxeter groups to $\mathbb Z$.

We give examples of right-angled Coxeter groups whose graphs do not satisfy the legal system criterion, but contain finite index right-angled Coxeter subgroups whose graphs admit legal systems.

We also provide a family of examples of graphs without legal systems, where no sequence of the considered graph operations yields a graph with a legal system.

Moreover, we show that for a bipartite graph and an orbit of non-empty states under the bipartite system of moves, the associated homomorphism from the commutator subgroup of the right-angled Coxeter group to $\mathbb Z$ has finitely generated kernel if and only if the system is legal.

items.title: Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy
items.summary:
It is not known whether a classical polynomial-time verifier can verify arbitrary polynomial-time quantum computations with an efficient quantum honest prover without computational assumptions. We show that, relative to a classical oracle, such verification is possible for a language beyond the polynomial hierarchy that is decided exactly in quantum polynomial time. The protocol is public-coin, with perfect completeness and soundness error at most 1/4.

To our knowledge, no language with such a proof system was previously proved to lie outside AM relative to an oracle. For every unbounded polynomial-time computable function, the oracle can be chosen so that the message count and the oracle query counts of the quantum algorithm, verifier, and honest prover are bounded by this function of the input length. The message count is optimal up to a constant factor, since for a suitable oracle every interactive proof system for the language uses at least a constant fraction of the messages of our protocol on infinitely many lengths, with a constant depending on its verifier.

The language is a variant of recursive Fourier sampling in which code tables encode secrets that address data tables. The tables are evaluated recursively, and the oracle stores only the leaves. The quantum algorithm recovers every secret exactly, and the verifier checks the prover's secrets recursively against random code entries.

The recursion restricts the input in a correlated way, as the same secret fixes the code bits and chooses the free coordinate, so Håstad's switching lemma does not apply. We prove a switching theorem for these restrictions, which may be of independent interest. For instances of sufficient height, no constant-depth circuit of size $2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}$ changes its output with probability above $2^{-Ω(n)}$ when the answer of a random instance is flipped by changing a single leaf.

items.title: Localization, cobordism, and twisted $χ_y$-genera of $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}$
items.summary: We use the method of equivariant localization to obtain a recursion for the cobordism-valued one-point psi-class intersections on $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}$, and hence the cobordism classes $[\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}]$. Restricting to the hyperbolic formal group law, we recover the Poincaré polynomials of $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}$ as a special case, and obtain new formulas for Hirzebruch $χ_y$-genera of $\overline{\mathcal{M}}_{0,n}$ twisted by tautological line bundles.

items.title: Generic tensor products are not maximal
items.summary:
We construct tensor products of uniform matroids which are strictly freer than their generic linear tensor products. In particular, the generic tensor product of two copies of $U_{7,9}$ is not maximal.

More generally, for every $a,b\ge2$, this holds for $U_{7,a+7}$ and $U_{7,b+7}$. The construction disproves the uniform tensor-product formulation of Mason's conjecture.

Its dual is a relaxation of an explicit circuit-hyperplane of a generic birigidity matroid. By the author's representability theorem, the resulting matroids are non-representable over every field.

We also obtain full-rank counterexamples to the Jackson--Tanigawa hyperconnectivity conjecture in every dimension $d\ge2$.

items.title: Iwahori Whittaker functions for unramified quasi-split groups
items.summary:
Let $\mathbf{G}$ be a connected unramified quasi-split reductive group defined over a nonarchimedean local field $F$.

This paper concerns the Iwahori Whittaker functions attached to the unramified principal series of $\mathbf{G}(F)$.

We introduce Demazure-Whittaker operators and show that in the non-split case they generate a Hecke algebra with unequal parameters that are determined by $\mathbf{G}$.

We then connect these operators to the Whittaker functions, establishing formulas for calculating all values for a basis of Iwahori Whittaker functions and giving a new proof of the Casselman-Shalika formula for the spherical Whittaker function.

In doing so we build on the work for split groups of Brubaker, Bump and Licata; the new feature here is the appearance of a Hecke algebra with unequal parameters.

items.title: On $\mathbb{P}^1$-bundles on $\mathbb{P}^3$ that are small modifications of a Fano fourfold
items.summary:
We find necessary conditions for the projectivization of a rank two vector bundle $\mathcal{E}$ on $\mathbb{P}^3_{\mathbb{C}}$ to be related to a smooth Fano 4-fold by a small $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial modification (SQM).

Furthermore, we fully describe the birational geometry of $\mathbb{P}_{\mathbb{P}^3}(\mathcal{E})$ when $\mathcal{E}$ is stable, with $c_1=-1$, $c_2=2$.

In this case, we prove that there exists a flip from $X^+$ to $\mathbb{P}_{\mathbb{P}^3}(\mathcal{E})$, where $X^+$ is smooth and Fano.

We also determine the birational geometry and numerical invariants of $X^+$.

items.title: QuantrolOx Raises €12 Million in Series A2
items.summary:
Insider Brief

QuantrolOx raised €12 million in a Series A2 round led by IW Capital, with EIC Fund co-investment, to expand its quantum hardware automation and training business internationally.

The company’s three products support quantum hardware development and calibration, practical workforce training, and superconducting quantum computing research and education.

The funding will support product deployments, expanded training offerings and growth of its U.S. team, following a Berkeley office opening and a five-year collaboration agreement with UC Berkeley.

PRESS RELEASE — QuantrolOx , University of Oxford spinout headquartered in Finland with offices in the UK, Netherlands, US and India, has raised €12 million in a Series A2 funding round led by IW Capital , with co-investment from the European Innovation Council (EIC) Fund . The round also includes participation from Voima Ventures , Serendipity Capital , Hoxton Ventures , and Transpose Capital .

The investment will accelerate QuantrolOx ’s commercial growth and international expansion, including its growing presence in North America following the opening of its first US office in Berkeley, California. The round brings QuantrolOx’s total funding to ~$31million or ~€28million.

As quantum computing moves towards industrial-scale development, two major challenges remain: automating increasingly complex quantum hardware and training the workforce needed to build and operate it.

items.title: GTFormer: A Syntax-Free Graph Network Alternative to Transformers for 8192$\times$ Length Extrapolation in Linear Time
items.summary:
Self-attention mechanisms have established the Transformer as the dominant backbone across natural language processing, source code intelligence, and automated theorem proving.

However, all-to-all pairwise token comparison enforces a quadratic $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ compute and memory barrier alongside severe softmax attention dilution as sequence length $N$ scales beyond the training horizon.

Inspired by recent advances in algebraic graph learning (\textbf{WPNet}), this work introduces \textbf{GTFormer}, a syntax-free hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) that replaces flat self-attention for general long-context sequence modeling.

GTFormer organizes raw token streams into a bounded-degree hierarchy combining a balanced binary reduction tree ($\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ depth), horizontal boundary-bridging shift edges, random expander shortcuts, multi-channel convex highway gating, and a top-down broadcast pass.

Across eight long-context code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks trained exclusively on sequences of length $N \le 512$, GTFormer extrapolates zero-shot to $N = 4{,}194{,}304$ ($8192\times$) on a single commodity GPU in linear $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, maintaining near-perfect accuracy where standard and RoPE Transformers suffer from out-of-distribution attention collapse and out-of-memory exhaustion.

items.title: Guest Post: The Next Threat to Encryption May Not Need a Quantum Computer
items.summary:
Guest Post by Ofir Joseph, Quantum Communication Researcher, University of Haifa, and Head of the Cybersecurity Program, Academic College of Tel Aviv–Yaffo , Prof. Irit Hadar, Dean, Faculty of Computer and Information Science & Director, Center for Cyber, Law and Policy, University of Haifa ; Sean Galantzan, Researcher, Tel Aviv University and Miriam Shtilman, Tal Ventures

A bank does not need to lose a password for its security to weaken. A new mathematical method could make a previously impractical attack feasible. Research involving artificial intelligence (AI) is bringing that possibility into sharper focus.

Online payments rely partly on public-key cryptography , also called asymmetric cryptography: methods using two related digital keys, one public and one secret. These keys are strings of data, not passwords. They help computers establish private connections and check who issued information. Their security depends on certain calculations remaining too difficult for attackers.

Much preparation has centred on quantum computers , which exploit the unusual behaviour of matter at very small scales to perform some calculations differently. A sufficiently capable machine could defeat widely used public-key methods. But better mathematical methods could also change the odds, with AI helping researchers find them.

What OpenAI reported

On 26 October 2026, OpenAI reported that its AI had refuted the Exponential

Time Hypothesis, a longstanding, unproved conjecture about how computation grows as problems become larger.

items.title: A note on data-efficient finetuning of vision foundation models
items.summary:
Adapting foundation models to a new task within or beyond the training domain is the de facto standard for building specialized machine learning models. Recently, Visual Prompting (VP) has emerged as a promising technique for efficient knowledge transfer.

As new foundation model families~(like Mamba) get introduced and VP pipelines such as AutoVP reach greater maturity, we find a growing need for a systematic evaluation of current approaches. In this work, we assess the performance of the latest models, comparing them to earlier architectures and alternative fine-tuning methods, to better understand the progress, challenges and opportunities in the field of efficient fine-tuning under resource limitations.

Towards this goal, this paper provides a concise empirical overview of the interactions among foundation model families (Attention-, Convolution-, and Mamba-based) and transfer paradigms: VP, Linear Probing (LP), Full Fine-tuning (FFT) and Low Rank Adaptation (LoRA). Our work builds up on previous findings by broadening the selection of evaluated models and techniques while tuning hyperparameters.

In the interest of delivering practical guidelines for the user, we also explore application of prevalent regularization techniques to boost performance in the context of VP.

items.title: Rank functions, $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extensions and class numbers
items.summary:
If $F$ is a number field and $F = F_0 \subset F_1 \subset F_2\subset \cdots$ is a tower of Galois extensions with $\mathrm{Gal}(F_n/F)$ cyclic of order $p^n$, K.

Iwasawa gave a closed formula for the growth of the $p$-part of the class number of $F_n$ whenever $n$ is large enough.

We present a new proof of this formula, obtained by reinterpreting its summands in terms of Sylvester matrix rank functions on the Iwasawa algebra $Λ$ without resorting to the classification of finitely-generated $Λ$-modules up to pseudo-isomorphism.

items.title: Can we trust LLMs to judge whether a research idea is novel?
items.summary:
Today we’re releasing Old Ideas, Novel Problems , a new study of how reliably large language models can evaluate the novelty of scientific research ideas. Alongside the paper, we’re publishing a benchmark, data, and code for testing novelty judges, plus an automated pipeline researchers can use to build new evaluation sets.

At Ai2, we’ve been developing AI systems that support different parts of scientific discovery. DataVoyager helps researchers explore and analyze structured data, AutoDiscovery generates and tests hypotheses, and Theorizer synthesizes evidence across large bodies of literature into candidate scientific theories. Together with Asta , these projects point toward systems that can help researchers move from understanding prior work to proposing, testing, and refining new ideas.

But generating research ideas is only part of the challenge of automating scientific discovery. Those ideas also need to contribute something genuinely new, which means these systems need a way to distinguish a novel direction from one that mostly repackages existing work.

That judgment is often handed to another LLM—what we call a novelty judge . Novelty judges assess whether a research idea is new relative to prior work, either on its own or in comparison with another idea. There’s no standard way to build one; research teams choose a model, prompt, evaluation format, reasoning budget, and sometimes a literature-retrieval system. Those choices can materially affect the verdict. Yet these judges are often validated only on human-written papers rather than the AI-generated ideas they are actually meant to evaluate.

Our new benchmark results suggest novelty evaluation itself is far from reliable. Across six LLM judges – GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.6 – seemingly small changes to the evaluation setup produce dramatically different judgments of the same ideas. In one experiment, changing just a few words in a prompt shifts a model’s accuracy in identifying which of two ideas is more novel by more than 50 percentage points. Retrieval and additional reasoning do not consistently improve judgments, and two purpose-built novelty evaluation systems perform worse than a simple prompted Claude Opus 4.6 baseline.

items.title: On a problem of A. N. Skiba and L. A. Shemetkov concerning $S_n$-closed subformations of a one-generated formation
items.summary:
Throughout this paper, all groups are finite. Let $\mathrm{form}(G)$ denote the formation generated by a group $G$. A formation $\mathfrak{F}$ is said to be $S_n$-closed if every subnormal subgroup of every group in $\mathfrak{F}$ belongs to $\mathfrak{F}$.

A. N. Skiba and L.

A. Shemetkov posed the problem of proving that $\mathrm{form}(G)$ has only finitely many $S_n$-closed subformations for every group $G$ (Problem 14.81 of the Kourovka Notebook). In this paper we propose a negative answer to this problem.

We prove that for the group $G_0=(\mathrm{SL}_2(5)\rtimes C_2)\times\mathrm{SL}_2(5)$ of order 28800, where $C_2$ acts on $\mathrm{SL}_2(5)$ by an outer automorphism, the formation $\mathrm{form}(G_0)$ has an infinite strictly descending chain of $S_n$-closed subformations. The main tool is a family of central-valued multilinear maps, defined for every group in $\mathrm{form}(G_0)$ by its outer actions on its components; their vanishing is preserved under taking epimorphic images, subdirect products and subnormal subgroups. The members of the chain are separated by central quotients of the groups $\mathrm{SL}_2(5)^{2^d-1}\rtimes C_2^d$, $d\geq 2$.

Using Burichenko's description of the lattice of subformations of $\mathrm{form}(\mathrm{SL}_2(5)\rtimes C_2)$, we also prove that every non-empty $S_n$-closed subformation of $\mathrm{form}(G_0)$ is generated, as an ordinary formation, by a single group, and that the set of such subformations is countably infinite. Finally, we determine the intersection of the chain and give an explicit generator of it.

items.title: Rank reduction in orthosymplectic types
items.summary:
This note establishes a rank reduction for RLL-realization of quantum affine supergroups of orthosymplectic type.

In the rational limit, this provides a more conceptual proof of the analogous result for orthosymplectic superYangians from arXiv:2311.18818.

We also determine the exact scalar prefactor appearing in the evaluation of the universal $R$-matrix, refining the main result of arXiv:2408.16720.

items.title: CRISP: Co-designing Pruning and Scheduling for Efficient MoE Inference on Edge Servers
items.summary:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference on memory-constrained edge platforms is often dominated by expert-weight movement rather than computation. Although each token activates only a small subset of experts, routing is input-dependent, so all experts must remain accessible and memory movement dominates latency.

Existing approaches such as uniform pruning and expert dropping overlook two properties of MoE execution: expert combinations are highly skewed in frequency, and experts contribute asymmetrically within each combination. We present CRISP, a combination-aware framework that co-designs pruning and runtime scheduling for efficient MoE serving on memory-constrained edge platforms.

CRISP reorders neurons by importance so one stored expert can support multiple execution widths, assigns differentiated execution to hot, warm, and cold combinations based on frequency and expert role, and exploits heterogeneous widths to overlap expert loading with computation. Across Mixtral-8x7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B, CRISP improves throughput by up to $2.1\times$ at the same memory budget while limiting accuracy loss to 3.6\% relative to full-width inference.

Our results highlight that efficient edge MoE serving requires jointly optimizing which expert capacity is preserved and how expert execution is scheduled.

items.title: Representation and abelianization growth, particularly along expanding sequences
items.summary:
We study two obstructions to a finite group $G$ having a generating $d$-tuple whose Cayley graph has spectral gap at least $ε$. Lubotzky and Weiss proved that such a gap forces $\mathrm{ab}_k(G)$, the largest order of the abelianization of a subgroup of index at most $k$, to be $\exp(O_ε(dk))$, while de la Harpe, Robertson and Valette proved that it forces $\mathrm{rep}_k(G)$, the number of irreducible complex representations of degree at most $k$, to be $\exp(O_ε(dk^2))$.

We show that the first bound implies the second, and in fact implies it with $k^2$ replaced by $k\log k$. For this, we prove that every finite $d$-generated group satisfies the inequality $\mathrm{rep}_k(G)\leq\exp((d-1)k\log k+O(dk))\cdot\mathrm{ab}_k(G)$, regardless of its spectral gap.

The leading term $(d-1)k\log k$ is attained by powers of alternating groups, and it disappears for groups without large alternating sections. The proof reduces to counting the finite primitive subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_m(\mathbf{C})$, and we show that there are at most $\exp(O(\log^4m))$ of them up to conjugacy and scalars.

Wigderson asked whether $k^2$ in the second bound can be lowered to $k$, so our result answers his question up to a logarithm. We do not know whether the logarithm is actually needed.

For powers of alternating groups, the natural candidates, we show that a spectral gap keeps the number of factors a fixed power below the maximum allowed by $d$-generation, and that random generators have spectral gap tending to $0$ already for superpolynomially many factors.

items.title: Finite group actions on the non-minimal nilpotent orbit closures in type A
items.summary:
We study quotients of the closures of the nilpotent orbits of type A by finite groups of inner automorphisms.

Assuming the nilpotent orbit is not minimal, we show that the Q-factorial terminalizations of quotients of nilpotent orbit closures are precisely the quotients of the symplectic resolutions of the orbit closures.

This identifies the Mori fan of each Q-factorial terminalization of the quotient with the Mori fan of a symplectic resolution of the orbit closure.

items.title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data
items.summary:
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data.

We show that channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads, because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks.

Second, top-k keeps each token's k highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data. At the calibrated budget, a selector's top-k version matches or beats its threshold version on the same score in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets, including all 23 on generation tasks.

The top-k versions also avoid the repetition-loop collapse that calibrated thresholds cause on Gemma 4. Calibrating a threshold thus provides neither of the two things selectors use it for: a known read budget and a consistent accuracy gain at that budget.

We furthermore introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights, which screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers the skipped ones with a low-rank map. Across three post-trained MoE models, our reader retains 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with Triton kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized vLLM at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches on the same three models.

items.title: Toric Varieties from Multiple Zeta Values
items.summary:
The linear relations among fixed weight multiple zeta values (MZVs) are a well-studied subject in number theory. Elements of putative linear bases for this fixed-weight space are, however, not algebraically independent; they satisfy non-linear relations.

We study these relations by approximating them through motivic MZVs, formal MZVs and numerical computations. We show that motivic MZVs in fixed weight span a projective toric variety and explore its geometry.

We define an outer approximation to the variety of formal MZVs in fixed weight by introducing toric varieties coming from shuffle and stuffle relations and taking their intersection. We conjecture that this intersection in fact agrees with the variety of formal MZVs and hence conjecturally also with the variety of motivic MZVs.

This leads to a novel conjecture on a generating set for the extended double shuffle relations, which we checked computationally up to weight $23$.

items.title: Measurement incompatibility and noiseless quantum codes
items.summary:
We construct a rank-one minimal informationally complete measurement (MIC) with an invertible dual operator and prove that, for arbitrary finite input and output dimensions, a channel universally preserves measurement incompatibility if and only if its input space contains a noiseless code subspace of the full output dimension. Preserving the compatibility threshold of a finite family of binary measurements already guarantees such a code.

Furthermore, for every $d\ge2$, there exists a family of binary measurements that is incompatible on the full space but compatible after compression to any proper subspace. These results resolve the conjecture of Chitambar and Zhang and the existence question posed by Uola and coauthors.

We also give an explicit construction of exact encodings and show that, for a sufficiently small shift in the compatibility threshold, the transmission error of an approximate encoding is bounded by a constant times the square of the shift. These results establish a connection between measurement compatibility, quantum steering, and quantum error correction.

items.title: CoS-VQ: Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization for Large Language Models
items.summary:
Large language models (LLMs) require substantial memory, motivating low-bit weight quantization for efficient deployment. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods often improve accuracy by increasing the effective coding dimension, which can complicate independent lookup and local codeword updates.

We propose CoS-VQ (Coordinated Shared-Scale Vector Quantization), which preserves low-dimensional codewords while jointly optimizing hard indices and their shared scale across positions. The key challenge is scale-induced coupling: the optimal scale depends on the entire codeword combination and, in turn, changes candidate rankings across positions, so pointwise updates can stall even after scale re-optimization.

CoS-VQ collects candidates at multiple probe scales and constructs a tangent separable upper bound for the residual-aware quadratic objective. By reducing candidate comparisons to lower envelopes of lines over positive scales, it identifies finitely many representative intervals for joint index--scale updates without exhaustively enumerating codeword combinations.

On Qwen3.8-27B, CoS-VQ outperforms QTIP and LLVQ on the evaluated language modeling, coding, and reasoning benchmarks. Ablations from the same initialization further show larger gains from joint updates than from scale-only refinement, highlighting joint selection as an alternative to increasing codeword dimensionality.

The code is available at https://github.com/xzktx003/Cos_VQ.

items.title: Irrationality of the conjugacy growth on Heisenberg groups
items.summary:
We demonstrate that the conjugacy growth series for the Heisenberg groups $H_n(\mathbb{Z})$ is never algebraic, irrespective of the generating set.

This makes progress towards the conjecture that all finitely presented groups that are not virtually abelian have irrational conjugacy growth series.

Contrary to the group $H_3(\mathbb{Z})$, where the conjugacy growth is $n^2\log(n)$, the conjugacy growth of the other Heisenberg groups is polynomial, making these groups the first known nilpotent groups where the irrationality does not follow from the asymptotic growth.

items.title: Localization of weighted Goldman volume on $\mathrm{SL}(3,\R)$-Hitchin Component
items.summary:
We compute Goldman volume on the moduli space of convex real projective structures on a closed oriented surface of genus at least two, with exponential weight defined by the shifted Blaschke area.

For every positive parameter, the integral converges and is a finite sum of inverse powers of that parameter.

Its coefficients are intersection numbers involving the bundle of regular cubic differentials on the moduli stack of stable curves.

The proof establishes absolute convergence and vanishing signed boundary integrals of the transgression under simultaneous plumbing degeneration.

The pushforward of Goldman measure by the shifted Blaschke area therefore has a polynomial density on $[0,\infty)$, and its sublevel volumes are polynomial in the threshold.

items.title: Non-split groups of Lie type and iSchur algebras with unequal parameters
items.summary:
We present a geometric framework for realizing quantum Schur algebras with unequal parameters, via constructible sheaves on flag varieties arising from non-split groups of Lie type. In the special cases of general unitary groups and minus-type orthogonal groups, this framework yields the iSchur algebras with unequal parameters, which are closely related to the quasi-split iquantum groups of type AIII.

Such a geometric realization enables the construction of canonical bases, integral forms, and monoidal categorification for these unequal-parameter iSchur algebras and the corresponding iquantum groups. This material is not a formal generalization from the equal-parameter case to the unequal-parameter case.

A nontrivial arithmetic structure is imposed on the geometric structure of split groups, giving rise to many new phenomena. For example, the support varieties of generators of an integral form may not be rationally smooth, the categorification is provided by the category of descent data of semisimple complexes fixed by the twisted Frobenius, and the positivity of the canonical basis is established using a refined covering.

items.title: Effective Gromov-Witten computations for GKM spaces and a semisimple application
items.summary:
We report a major update to our original software GKMtools and record multiple improvements in the computation of Gromov--Witten invariants of GKM spaces.

This includes a refined divisor equation that reduces the complexity from exponential to linear in the number of marked points, three tricks to accelerate the computation of curve class relations in the GKM graph, and an implementation of Mihalcea's algorithm for homogeneous varieties using the equivariant quantum Chevalley formula.

As an application, we prove that the small quantum cohomology of the type-$E$ generalized Grassmannians $E_7/P_2,E_7/P_4,E_7/P_5,E_8/P_6$ is generically semisimple.

These are precisely the remaining exceptional Grassmannians for which generic semisimplicity of small quantum cohomology was still unknown.

items.title: Deployed entanglement-based BBM92 quantum key distribution using frequency-converted photons emitted by a quantum dot
items.summary:
Establishing secure communication is an important requirement in existing and future networks. Although current solutions rely on classical approaches, quantum mechanics offers the possibility of moving from computational to information-theoretic security.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) has been extensively studied as a means of achieving such security. Recently, epitaxial quantum dots started to be studied and employed in quantum cryptography, because of their rapid development that made them one of the brightest sources of quantum light to date.

In particular, they are known to be excellent sources of polarization-entangled photon pairs, especially droplet-etched dots operating at $\sim$780 nm. Here, we employ such a quantum dot to generate entangled photon pairs under 1 GHz excitation rate.

Using quantum frequency conversion, we interface the emitted photons with the telecommunication wavelength range while preserving their polarization entanglement. This enables quantum key distribution over a 1.59 km field-deployed fibre link across the University of Stuttgart - campus Vaihingen, using the BBM92 protocol: we achieve a secure key rate of 206 Hz over 19 h of stable operation, resulting in a total secure key length of 14.2 Mbit.

This key enables the safe encryption and decryption of a colour image with further implementation of error correction and privacy amplification. These results demonstrate important steps towards hybrid quantum networks by combining high-quality entangled-photon sources operated at high excitation rates, efficient frequency conversion module, and picosecond-level time synchronization in a realistic deployed network.

items.title: Watermark Basins: Black-Box Detection of Distilled LLMs
items.summary:
Proprietary language models and their reasoning traces are vulnerable to API-based distillation, where an adversary trains a student model on the teacher model's outputs. To obtain evidence of distillation, model providers can watermark the teacher's outputs, aiming to leave a radioactive signal in the student's outputs.

Existing black-box detectors search for such radioactivity using token-level statistics of the suspect model's outputs. However, token-level signals are not always detectable, for instance when the distillation traces are sampled at a low temperature.
